lessons.title: The heart and circulatory system
objectives: Describe the function of the heart, blood vessels and blood
Name the three types of blood vessel
Explain how blood circulates around the body

keywords.def: a muscular pump that pushes blood around the body
a blood vessel carrying blood away from the heart
a blood vessel carrying blood back to the heart
a tiny blood vessel that exchanges materials with cells

starter: Bismillah. Name the colours of the spectrum.
Put your hand on your chest. What can you feel?
Why does the body need oxygen?

teach.heading: The circulatory system
teach.note: Link to previous work on digestion: nutrients from the small intestine enter the blood. The heart is a muscle, about the size of a fist.

teach.heading: The heart
bullets: Right side: blood to the lungs
Left side: blood to the body
teach.note: Keep it simple: the right side sends blood to pick up oxygen from the lungs, the left side pumps blood around the body. Valves stop backflow. Show a diagram.

teach.heading: Blood vessels
teach.note: Mnemonic: Arteries Away. Misconception: arteries always carry oxygen-rich blood; the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood. Keep this for GCSE, but be ready if asked.

teach.heading: Pulse
bullets: Find your pulse in the wrist
teach.note: Safe task: children find their pulse using two fingers (not the thumb) on the wrist or neck, count for 15 seconds and multiply by four. Resting rate for children is typically between 70 and 100 beats per minute.

practice: What is the job of the heart?
Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
You count 20 beats in 15 seconds. What is the pulse rate per minute?
independent: Draw a simple diagram of the circulatory system with the heart, arteries, veins and capillaries labelled.
Write what blood carries to the body and what it takes away.
Measure and record your resting pulse three times and find the average.
exit: Name the three types of blood vessel.
lessons.homework: Measure your resting pulse at the same time each day for three days and record it in a table.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a labelled heart diagram and key word cards. Stretch: explain why capillary walls are only one cell thick.

lessons.title: Diet, drugs and lifestyle
objectives: Describe how diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle affect the body
Explain the difference between helpful and harmful drugs
Make healthy choices and explain them

keywords.def: a substance that changes how the body works
a drug used to treat illness, taken safely as directed
the way a person lives, including diet, activity and sleep
can damage health

starter: Bismillah. What happens to your pulse during exercise?
Name two foods that give energy.

teach.heading: A healthy lifestyle
teach.note: Link back to nutrition in Year 3. Primary-age children need roughly 9 to 11 hours of sleep a night.

teach.heading: Medicines
bullets: Medicines help when we are ill
teach.note: Emphasise safety: only a trusted adult gives medicine. Paracetamol example is fine, but avoid dose information.

teach.heading: Harmful substances
bullets: Tobacco harms the lungs and heart
Alcohol harms the body and is forbidden in Islam
Caffeine and energy drinks are not for children
teach.note: Keep age-appropriate and factual. Link: Islam encourages protecting our bodies and minds, and intoxicants are forbidden (Qur'an 5:90). Do not frighten; give clear safe responses.

teach.heading: Making good choices
teach.note: Role play a short scenario of being offered something unsafe. Practise a confident reply. Remind pupils that they can always speak to a teacher, parent or imam.

practice: Give one example of a medicine and one rule for taking it safely.
Which organ is harmed by smoking?
What could you say if someone offered you something unsafe?
independent: Make a poster with five rules for a healthy lifestyle.
Write a short script of a safe response to an unsafe offer.
Explain in your own words why sleep is important.
exit: Who can you talk to if you are worried about a drug?
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about one healthy habit they keep, and write what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a pictorial poster template. Stretch: evaluate a day's choices in a diary and suggest improvements.

lessons.title: Review: light and the circulatory system
objectives: Recall key facts about light, the heart and a healthy lifestyle
Apply knowledge to new questions
Identify areas to improve

keywords.def: light bouncing off a surface
light bending as it moves between materials
the movement of blood around the body
the beat of the heart felt in the wrist or neck

starter: Bismillah. State two facts about light.
State two facts about the heart.

teach.heading: Light review
bullets: Reflection: angle in equals angle out
teach.note: Quick questioning. Ask children to explain how we see, using arrows into the eye. Correct the common misconceptions again.

teach.heading: Heart review
teach.note: Ask children to draw the circulation on mini whiteboards. Check that they say 'away from the heart' for arteries.

teach.heading: Healthy lifestyle review
teach.note: Link back to previous lessons. Ask: 'What would you advise a friend?' Encourage respectful and kind answers.

teach.heading: Applying ideas
bullets: A tall person casts a long shadow
A swimmer's pulse after a race
A rainbow on a sunny, rainy day
teach.note: Use unfamiliar contexts so children must explain with science words. Model one answer in full sentences with 'because'.

practice: Explain why a red jumper looks red in white light.
A boy's pulse is 70 at rest and 120 after running. Explain why.
A ray hits a mirror at 25 degrees to the normal. State the reflected angle.
independent: Complete a 10-question quiz on light, the heart and lifestyle.
Write three things you remember well and one you need to revise.
Make a mind map linking light, the eye, and the heart.
exit: Name one thing you are confident about.
Name one thing you will practise.
lessons.homework: Revise using your mind map and teach one idea to a family member.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the quiz with picture support. Stretch: write three exam-style questions with answers for a partner.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Living things and their habitats (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: What is classification?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do scientists sort living things into groups?
objectives: To understand why and how we classify things using their features
successCriteria: All: sort objects into groups using one feature
Most: sort the same objects in two different ways
Some: explain why scientists need one agreed way to classify
lessons.crossCurricular: Computing: sorting data with yes/no questions
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the order and variety in Allah's creation

keywords.def: sort into groups by shared features
a part or quality we can observe
things that share a feature
look closely and notice details
the rules used to sort

hook.text: A library sorts books so you can find them fast. How might sorting living things help a scientist?
hook.a: It makes them easier to name, study and compare, and shows how they are alike.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Allah has created every animal from water. Of them are some that creep on their bellies, some that walk on two legs, and some that walk on four' (an-Nur 24:45). Noticing how creatures are alike and different is part of reflecting on creation.

starter.q: An animal with a backbone is a...

starter.a: The natural home of a living thing.

teach.heading: Why classify?
bullets: Millions of kinds of living things
Groups make them easier to study
Shared features show how they are alike
teach.note: Ask: how does a supermarket help you find food? It groups it.

teach.heading: Sort household objects
teach.note: Use a spoon, a pencil, a sock, a cup, a coin, a leaf.

teach.heading: Good features to use
bullets: Must have a clear yes or no
teach.note: Opinions do not work: two people would sort differently.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which is a good feature for classifying animals?
check.why: A backbone can be observed and has a clear yes or no answer.

practice.q: Sort: robin, bee, bat, ant using 'has wings?'
practice.a: Wings: robin, bee, bat. No wings: ant (most ants).
practice.model:
Ask the question for each one.
Robin: wings, yes.
Bee: yes.
Bat: yes.
Ant: worker ants have no wings.
So three in one group, ant in the other.

practice.q: Why is 'is it big?' a poor question?
practice.a: People would disagree; it is an opinion, not a clear feature.

practice.q: What does 'classify' mean?
practice.a: Sort into groups by shared features.

independent.q: Core: Collect 8 objects at home. Sort them two different ways and record both in tables.
independent.a: Pupils' own; e.g. by material and by use.
independent.model: Teacher shows one way first: by material (metal, plastic, fabric).

independent.q: Extend: Sort these animals with two questions: cat, eagle, goldfish, snake, frog, owl.
independent.a: For example: feathers? (eagle, owl); then fur? (cat); the rest: goldfish, snake, frog.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do scientists all over the world need the same system?
independent.a: So they can share findings and know they mean the same living thing.

exit.q: A good sorting question has...
exit.a: A) a clear yes or no

exit.q: Big question: why do scientists sort living things into groups?
exit.a: To make millions of living things easier to name, study and compare.

lessons.homework: Sort the food in one kitchen cupboard into groups. Write your criteria.
lessons.send: SEND: two-group sort with picture cards. EAL: feature, group, sort. Stretch: sort the same objects three ways.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Living things and their habitats (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: The five kingdoms and Carl Linnaeus
lessons.bigQuestion: How did Linnaeus give every living thing a name that scientists everywhere understand?
objectives: To understand how living things are grouped into kingdoms and named with two-part names
successCriteria: All: name the five kingdoms
Most: put living things into the right kingdom
Some: explain how Linnaeus's two-part names work
lessons.crossCurricular: History: scientists of the 1700s and their methods
lessons.smsc: Cultural: science as shared knowledge across countries

keywords.def: the largest group of living things
a Swedish scientist who made a naming system
one kind of living thing
a small group of closely related species
a two-part scientific name

hook.text: A 'robin' in Britain and a 'robin' in America are different birds. How could scientists avoid that mix-up?
hook.a: Give each species one scientific name used everywhere.

starter.q: What makes a good sorting question?
starter.a: It has a clear yes or no answer.

teach.heading: Five kingdoms
teach.note: This is the five-kingdom system taught in schools.

teach.heading: Fungi are not plants
bullets: They cannot make their own food
They feed on dead or living things
teach.note: Common error: mushrooms are plants.

misconception.right: A mushroom is a fungus: it has no chlorophyll and cannot make its own food

teach.heading: Carl Linnaeus (1707 to 1778)
bullets: Gave each species a two-part name
teach.note: Explain genus then species, written in italics.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which kingdom does yeast belong to?
check.why: Yeast is a single-celled fungus.

practice.q: Polar bear: Ursus maritimus. Which word is the genus?
practice.a: Ursus.
practice.model:
The first word is the genus, with a capital letter.
The second is the species.
So Ursus is the genus.

practice.q: Which kingdom: an oak tree?
practice.a: Plants.

practice.q: Why do polar bears and brown bears share 'Ursus'?
practice.a: They are closely related (the same genus).

independent.q: Core: Put 10 living things into the five kingdoms: mushroom, moss, earthworm, yeast, penguin, oak, amoeba, bread mould, Lactobacillus (in yoghurt), seaweed.
independent.a: Fungi: mushroom, yeast, bread mould. Plants: moss, oak. Animals: earthworm, penguin. Protoctists: amoeba, seaweed (some classifications). Bacteria: Lactobacillus.
independent.model: Teacher sorts two first: penguin (animal: eats food, moves), moss (plant: green, makes its own food).

independent.q: Extend: Write three facts about Linnaeus's naming system.
independent.a: Two parts; genus then species; same name used worldwide.

independent.q: Stretch: Why are scientific names in Latin rather than English or Arabic?
independent.a: Latin was the shared language of scholars in Europe at the time, so no one country's language was favoured.

exit.q: Linnaeus came from...
exit.a: A) Sweden

exit.q: Big question: how did Linnaeus give every living thing a name scientists everywhere understand?
exit.a: A two-part Latin name: genus and species, used worldwide.

lessons.homework: Find the scientific name of two animals that live in polar regions and write what group each belongs to.
lessons.send: SEND: kingdom picture cards. EAL: kingdom, fungus, genus, species. Stretch: research one Muslim scholar who wrote about animals, such as al-Jahiz's Book of Animals.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Living things and their habitats (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: Vertebrates and invertebrates
lessons.bigQuestion: What has a skeleton on the outside?
objectives: To understand how the animal kingdom is divided into vertebrates and invertebrate groups
successCriteria: All: sort animals into vertebrates and invertebrates
Most: name invertebrate groups such as insects, arachnids and molluscs
Some: use features to explain where a tricky animal belongs
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: Venn diagrams for sorting
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the vast number of small creatures Allah has made

keywords.def: an animal with a backbone
an animal without a backbone
an invertebrate with six legs and three body parts
an invertebrate with eight legs, such as a spider
a soft-bodied invertebrate, often with a shell

hook.text: Nearly all the animals on Earth have no backbone. Can you name five?
hook.a: Insects, spiders, worms, snails, jellyfish, crabs and many more.

starter.q: Which kingdom is a mushroom in?
Who made the two-part naming system?

teach.heading: Vertebrate groups
teach.note: Quick recap from Year 5; Arctic examples: seal (mammal), snowy owl (bird), Arctic char (fish).

teach.heading: Invertebrate groups
teach.note: Krill in polar seas are crustaceans.

teach.heading: Outside skeletons
bullets: Insects and crabs have an exoskeleton
A hard case on the outside
teach.note: Answer to the big question.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: A spider is an...
check.why: Spiders have eight legs and two body parts: arachnids.

practice.q: Is a krill a vertebrate or an invertebrate? Which group?
practice.a: Invertebrate; a crustacean.
practice.model:
Does it have a backbone?
No, it has a hard outer shell.
So it is an invertebrate.
Hard shell and many legs: crustacean.

practice.q: How many legs does an insect have?
practice.a: Six.

practice.q: Is a squid a mollusc?
practice.a: Yes (soft body).

independent.q: Core: Sort 12 animals (portal card set) into vertebrate groups and invertebrate groups.
independent.a: Answers in the card set key.
independent.model: Teacher sorts two first: seal (fur, milk: mammal), beetle (6 legs: insect).

independent.q: Extend: Is a woodlouse an insect? Explain using features.
independent.a: No: it has 14 legs; it is a crustacean.

independent.q: Stretch: Draw a Venn diagram for 'lives in water' and 'has a backbone' with 8 animals.
independent.a: Accept a correct Venn, e.g. both: seal, fish; water only: jellyfish, krill.

exit.q: Six legs and three body parts means an...
exit.a: A) insect

exit.q: Big question: what has a skeleton on the outside?
exit.a: Invertebrates such as insects and crabs: an exoskeleton.

lessons.homework: Find three invertebrates near your home (do not harm them) and say which group each belongs to.
lessons.send: SEND: count legs on picture cards. EAL: legs, shell, backbone. Stretch: research a polar invertebrate.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Living things and their habitats (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: Micro-organisms: helpful and harmful
lessons.bigQuestion: Are all germs bad?
objectives: To understand that micro-organisms are tiny living things that can be helpful or harmful
successCriteria: All: name bacteria, fungi and viruses as micro-organisms
Most: give one helpful and one harmful example
Some: explain safely how mould grows on bread
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and technology: yeast in bread and bacteria in yoghurt
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: Allah sends a cure for every disease

keywords.def: a living thing too small to see without a microscope
tiny single cells; some help, some cause disease
a living thing such as yeast, mould or a mushroom
a tiny germ that can only reproduce inside living cells
a fungus that grows on old food

hook.text: Bread, yoghurt and some medicines are made with the help of tiny living things. How could something too small to see be useful?
hook.a: Yeast makes bread rise; bacteria turn milk into yoghurt; some fungi make antibiotics.

islamicLink.text: The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah has not sent down a disease except that He has also sent down its cure' (Sahih al-Bukhari). Learning about micro-organisms helps people find cures and stay healthy.

starter.q: How many legs does an insect have?

teach.heading: Tiny living things
bullets: Too small to see without a microscope
Viruses are germs that need living cells
teach.note: Scientists argue whether viruses are alive: they cannot grow on their own.

teach.heading: Helpful or harmful?
teach.note: Sort together.

teach.heading: Bread mould in a sealed bag
bullets: Damp bread in a sealed clear bag
teach.note: Mould spores can make some people ill. Observe through the bag only; an adult disposes of it.
cycle: Damp and warm help them grow

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Which micro-organism makes bread rise?
check.why: Yeast feeds on sugar and gives off carbon dioxide gas, which makes dough rise.

practice.q: Give one helpful micro-organism and what it does.
practice.a: For example: yeast makes bread rise.
practice.model:
Name it: yeast.
Say the job: makes bread rise.
Say how: it gives off gas bubbles.
So: yeast is helpful because it makes bread rise.

practice.q: Why do we wash our hands before eating?
practice.a: To remove harmful bacteria and viruses.

practice.q: Why must the mould bag stay sealed?
practice.a: Mould spores can make people ill if breathed in.

independent.q: Core: Set up the mould bag with an adult (a slice of bread, a few drops of water, sealed bag). Draw it on day 1 and plan when to observe it again.
independent.a: Day 1 drawing; observe on days 3, 5 and 7 through the bag.
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: dampen the bread with three drops of water, seal, label with the date, put in a warm place.

independent.q: Extend: Predict: will mould grow faster in a warm or a cold place? Why?
independent.a: Warm: micro-organisms grow faster in warmth.

independent.q: Stretch: Why do we keep food in the fridge?
independent.a: The cold slows the growth of bacteria and moulds.

exit.q: All micro-organisms are harmful.
exit.a: B) false

exit.q: Big question: are all germs bad?
exit.a: No: many micro-organisms are helpful, such as yeast and yoghurt bacteria.

lessons.homework: Observe your mould bag on days 3 and 5 through the bag. Draw and describe what you see. Then an adult throws it away sealed.
lessons.send: SEND: picture sort helpful and harmful. EAL: germ, mould, yeast, bacteria. Stretch: find out how Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Living things and their habitats (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: Polar habitats
lessons.bigQuestion: How is the Arctic different from the Antarctic, and from where we live?
objectives: To understand the conditions in polar habitats and how they differ from habitats near us
successCriteria: All: locate the Arctic and Antarctic on a globe
Most: describe three conditions of polar habitats
Some: compare a polar habitat with a local habitat
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: lines of latitude and the poles
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the alternation of night and day as a sign (long polar days and nights)

keywords.def: near the North or South Pole
the frozen ocean region around the North Pole
the icy continent around the South Pole
the natural home of a living thing
the usual weather of a place over many years

hook.text: In the Arctic summer the Sun does not set for weeks. How would you know when to pray?
hook.a: Muslims there follow scholars' guidance, often using the times of the nearest normal place or Makkah.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for people of understanding' (Al Imran 3:190). Near the poles, day and night can each last for months.

starter.a: For example: a cold virus or food poisoning bacteria.
The natural home of a living thing.

teach.heading: Two poles
bullets: Polar bears in the north, penguins in the south
teach.note: Common mix-up: polar bears and penguins never meet in the wild.

teach.heading: Polar conditions
bullets: Very cold, often below -30 °C in winter
Strong winds, little rain or snow
teach.note: Antarctica is the coldest, windiest and driest continent.

teach.heading: Compare
teach.note: Ask pupils to add their local park.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: Where do penguins live in the wild?
check.why: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere; polar bears live in the Arctic.

practice.q: Name two conditions of the Antarctic.
practice.a: For example: extremely cold, windy, dry, long dark winters.
practice.model:
Think about temperature, wind, water and light.
Very cold, strong winds.
So two conditions: extremely cold and very windy.

practice.q: Which pole is a frozen ocean?
practice.a: The Arctic.

practice.q: Why are there few plants in the Antarctic?
practice.a: It is too cold, dark and dry; there is little soil.

independent.q: Core: Make a comparison table: Arctic, Antarctic and your local area (temperature, land, plants, animals).
independent.a: Arctic: frozen sea, polar bears, seals; Antarctic: ice continent, penguins, seals; local: mild, woodland animals.
independent.model:
Teacher fills the first row: temperature.
Arctic: very cold; Antarctic: colder still; local: mild.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why fewer kinds of living things survive in polar habitats.
independent.a: Extreme cold, dark and lack of food and water mean only specially adapted living things survive.

independent.q: Stretch: Why is Antarctica colder than the Arctic?
independent.a: It is high, thick ice on land; the Arctic is ocean, which holds some warmth.

exit.q: Polar bears live in the...
exit.a: A) Arctic

exit.q: Big question: how is the Arctic different from the Antarctic and from where we live?
exit.a: The Arctic is a frozen ocean, the Antarctic an icy continent; both are far colder and darker than our habitats.

lessons.homework: Find the Arctic and Antarctic on a globe or map app and write the names of two countries that reach into the Arctic.
lessons.send: SEND: map with poles labelled; picture sort of polar and local animals. EAL: north, south, cold, ice. Stretch: research one Antarctic research station.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Living things and their habitats (Frozen Kingdom)
lessons.title: Polar food chains
lessons.bigQuestion: Why is tiny krill so important in the Antarctic?
objectives: To understand how energy passes through polar food chains
successCriteria: All: write a polar food chain with arrows
Most: label producer, consumer, predator and prey
Some: explain what would happen if krill numbers fell
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: the Southern Ocean
lessons.smsc: Moral: our duty to protect oceans from overfishing and pollution

keywords.def: shows what eats what, with arrows
makes its own food, like phytoplankton
tiny plant-like living things in the sea
small shrimp-like animals eaten by many sea creatures
the top predator, which nothing hunts

hook.text: A blue whale, the largest animal, eats creatures only about 5 cm long. How can that work?
hook.a: It eats huge numbers of krill at once.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people's hands have earned' (ar-Rum 30:41). Overfishing krill could damage the whole Antarctic food chain, so protecting it is part of our duty as caretakers.

starter.q: Every food chain starts with a...
What does the arrow in a food chain mean?
starter.a: 'Is eaten by': energy passes along it.

teach.heading: Southern Ocean chain
teach.note: Arrows show the direction of energy.

teach.heading: Arctic chain
bullets: Arctic cod → ringed seal → polar bear
teach.note: Polar bear is the apex predator in the Arctic.

teach.heading: Common error
teach.note: Correct the direction.

misconception.right: fish → seal (energy goes into the seal)

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds.

check.q: In phytoplankton → krill → penguin → leopard seal, the producer is...
check.why: Phytoplankton make their own food using sunlight.

practice.q: Write a chain with: polar bear, phytoplankton, ringed seal, Arctic cod, zooplankton.
practice.a: phytoplankton → zooplankton → Arctic cod → ringed seal → polar bear
practice.model:
Start with the producer: phytoplankton.
Then who eats it?
Zooplankton.
Then Arctic cod, then ringed seal, then the apex predator: polar bear.

practice.q: Name the apex predator in that chain.
practice.a: Polar bear.

practice.q: Is a penguin a predator, prey or both?
practice.a: Both: it eats krill and is eaten by leopard seals.

independent.q: Core: Use the polar animal cards to build two Antarctic food chains and label each living thing.
independent.a: For example: phytoplankton → krill → crabeater seal → orca; phytoplankton → krill → Adelie penguin → leopard seal.
independent.model:
Teacher builds the first: phytoplankton → krill → blue whale.
Label: producer, prey, predator.

independent.q: Extend: Explain what would happen to penguins and whales if krill were overfished.
independent.a: They would have less food, so their numbers could fall.

independent.q: Stretch: Join your chains into a food web. Why is a web more realistic?
independent.a: Most animals eat more than one thing, so chains link together.

exit.q: Krill eat...
exit.a: A) phytoplankton

exit.q: Big question: why is tiny krill so important in the Antarctic?
exit.a: So many animals eat krill that, without it, the whole food chain would struggle.

lessons.homework: Write a food chain for a habitat near you and one for the Arctic. Compare them in one sentence.
lessons.send: SEND: chain cards with arrows to order. EAL: eat, eaten by, top predator. Stretch: research why krill fishing is controlled.

An adult uses the oven if baking

check.q: A mould fossil is...
check.why: A mould is the hollow. A cast fills it.

practice.q: How is your model like a real fossil forming?
practice.a: The dough is like soft mud; the shell leaves a mould shape
practice.model: Match each part of the model to real life: dough = mud or sediment; pressing = being buried; the hollow = a mould fossil.

practice.q: How is the model different from real life?
practice.a: It takes minutes, not millions of years; no rock or minerals form

practice.q: What would fill a mould to make a cast?
practice.a: Minerals (in the model: more dough or plaster)

independent.q: Core: Make two mould fossils with different objects. Draw each and label it 'mould'.
independent.a: Two drawings of clear moulds, labelled
independent.model: Teacher presses a shell into dough on camera and draws the mould.

independent.q: Extend: Fill one mould with a little more dough, press and lift it out to make a cast. Draw it.
independent.a: A drawing of a raised cast the same shape as the object

independent.q: Stretch: Evaluate your model: one strength and one limitation.
independent.a: Strength: shows the shape kept in mud; limitation: no minerals and far too quick

exit.q: A solid copy made when minerals fill a mould is a...
exit.a: Cast

exit.q: Big question: what fills the hollow to make a stone copy?
exit.a: Minerals carried by water fill it over a long time: a cast fossil.

model.problem: Explain how a cactus is adapted to the desert.
steps: Feature: spines instead of leaves
What it does: less surface for water to escape
Link: so the cactus keeps water and survives the dry desert
model.answer: Spines reduce water loss, so the cactus survives where there is little rain.

teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: Which is inherited?
options: A fox's limp from an injury
check.why: Only fur colour passes from parents to young.

practice.q: Explain how a duck's webbed feet are an adaptation.
practice.a: Webbed feet push more water, so the duck swims well to find food and escape
practice.model: Feature: webbed feet. What it does: pushes against more water. Link: so it swims well to find food and survive.

practice.q: What does extinct mean?
practice.a: No longer living anywhere

independent.q: Q1: Give two examples of variation in cats.
independent.a: For example: fur colour, size
independent.model: Teacher reads Q1 aloud and models answering with two short examples.

independent.q: Q2: Sort: eye colour, a scar, beak shape. Inherited or surroundings?
independent.a: Inherited: eye colour, beak shape; surroundings: a scar

independent.q: Q3: Why are offspring not identical to their parents?
independent.a: They inherit a mix of characteristics from both parents

independent.q: Q4: Explain one adaptation of a polar bear (use 'so').
independent.a: Thick fur keeps it warm, so it survives the Arctic cold

independent.q: Q5: Put in order: survivors have young; moths vary; birds eat moths that stand out.
independent.a: Moths vary; birds eat moths that stand out; survivors have young

independent.q: Q6: Which rock usually holds fossils?
independent.a: Sedimentary rock

independent.q: Q7: How do fossils show that living things can become extinct?
independent.a: We find fossils of creatures that no longer live anywhere

independent.q: Q8: Write a full explanation of how a camel is adapted to the desert (written in the portal response box).
independent.a: For example: wide feet so it does not sink in sand; hump stores fat for energy; long eyelashes keep sand out

keywords.def: a scientific explanation based on evidence

facts that support or challenge an idea

hook.text: Two scientists working on opposite sides of the world had the same idea at almost the same time. Why might that happen?
hook.a: They both made careful observations of animals in many places and thought hard about the same evidence.

islamicLink.text: Muslims believe Allah is the Creator of every living thing. Allah tells us He created Adam, peace be upon him, the first human, from dust and then said to him 'Be', and he was (Al 'Imran 3:59). So Muslims do not accept that humans came from other animals. Changes we can observe within a kind of living thing, such as the colour of moths, happen only by Allah's will and decree.

starter.q: Natural selection means the best suited...

starter.a: Birds ate the ones that stood out
options: Birds ate the ones that stood out

teach.note: No pictures of people: use the map and the finches.

Darwin's and Wallace's papers presented together in London

bullets: Each island's finches had different beaks
Thick beaks crack seeds; thin beaks catch insects
teach.note: Darwin asked why the beaks differed.

teach.heading: Alfred Russel Wallace
bullets: Studied wildlife in South America and South-East Asia
Sent his ideas to Darwin in 1858

teach.heading: Observation or theory?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: 30 seconds. Launch the Teams poll.

check.q: 'Finches on different islands have different beaks' is...
check.why: It is something Darwin saw. The explanation he gave for it is the theory.

practice.q: Explain why finches that eat hard seeds have thick beaks.
practice.a: Thick, strong beaks crack hard seeds, so those finches get food and survive
practice.model: Feature: thick beak. What it does: cracks hard seeds. Link: so the finch gets food and survives.

practice.q: Name the ship Darwin sailed on.
practice.a: HMS Beagle

practice.q: Who else had the idea of natural selection?
practice.a: Alfred Russel Wallace

independent.q: Core: Make a fact file on Darwin and Wallace: where they travelled, what they observed and what they explained. (Facts only; no portraits.)
independent.a: A fact file with places, observations and the idea of natural selection
independent.model: Teacher fills in Darwin's row: 'HMS Beagle; Galapagos finch beaks; natural selection'.

independent.q: Extend: Sort five statements into observation or theory.
independent.a: Observations: what was seen; theory: the explanation

independent.q: Stretch: Why do scientists share ideas, as Darwin and Wallace did in 1858?
independent.a: So others can check the evidence and test the idea

exit.q: A scientific explanation based on evidence is a...
exit.a: Theory

exit.q: Big question: why might two scientists have the same idea at once?
exit.a: They studied similar evidence carefully in many places.
